title: Management of Opportunistic Infections in HIV

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of fevers, cough, and hemoptysis. He was known to have untreated HIV . Investigations: Sputum microscopy: numerous AFBs seen CD4 count 155 cells/μ L He was started on 4-drug antimycobacterial therapy.
questions.lead_in: When is the most appropriate time to introduce ART?
questions.explanation: 4 weeks Due to the potential for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), timing of ART initiation in patients with tuberculosis infection may need to be delayed until effective anti-TB therapy has been instituted. Based on available evidence for nonmeningeal TB infections, current HIV treatment guidelines recommend that ART be started within 2 weeks for patients with a CD4 count <50 cells/μL and between 2 and 8 weeks for patients with a CD4 count >50 cells/μL.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q36

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with fevers and a neck lump. She had been started 6 weeks earlier on quadruple antituberculous treatment for TB lymphadenitis and combination ART . She had initially improved on treatment, but then her fevers returned, and she noticed worsening enlargement and pain at the site of the involved lymph node. Investigations: Lymph node biopsy: granulomatous inflammation seen Lymph node culture: fully sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolated 1st visit 2nd visit CD4 count (cells/μL) 55 145 HIV viral load (copies/mL) 245,000 1,255
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Addition of a fifth anti-TB drug

questions.explanation: Addition of a nonsteroidal antiinflammatory This presentation would be most consistent with an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) from the TB lymphadenitis in a setting of rise in CD4 count and drop in HIV viral load with initiation of ART . Recommendations in most cases of TB IRIS are to continue ART and anti-TB therapy. In moderate to severe cases of IRIS, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs or corticosteroids can be added. The development of drug-resistant TB would be less likely at this time point, and surgical excision would not be recommended for a likely reversible and non-lifethreatening situation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q35

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presented with fever, productive cough, and weight loss. He was known to have HIV and was taking combination antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir-emtricitabine and darunavir boosted with ritonavir. Investigations: CXR: a single large cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe is seen, suspicious for pulmonary TB Sputum microscopy: numerous acid fast bacilli seen. Direct PCR positive for M. tuberculosis CD4 count 360 cells/μL HIV viral load <20 copies/mL
questions.explanation: Rifampin Due to significant drug interactions between boosted protease inhibitors and certain anti-TB drugs, modified regimens are often required. Rifampin, which is a potent CYP3A4 inducer, is contraindicated in the treatment of TB with patients on protease inhibitor-based HIV regimens. Rifabutin is a less potent CYP3A4 inducer so it can be used, with dose modification, in protease inhibitor-based regimens.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q38

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man attended for a new patient appointment. He had recently been diagnosed with HIV and had a history of allergic asthma and sulfa allergy, which caused a blistering rash with oral lesions. The patient was leaving the country for a 3-month business trip in 2 weeks’ time. Investigations: CD4 count 155 cells/mm3 HIV-1 RNA viral load 145,000 copies/mL Toxoplasma IgG positive Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase 3.4 U/gram of Hgb (8.8–13.4)
questions.lead_in: In addition to starting combination antiretroviral therapy, what antimicrobial prophylaxis is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Atovaquone PO once daily Given the patient’s CD4 count <200 cells/μL, prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia is indicated. The history of severe sulfa allergy and evidence of G-6-PD deficiency are contraindications to the use of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole or dapsone therapy. The patient’s history of asthma and travel plans limiting ability to return monthly for treatments also make the use of aerosolized pentamidine less attractive. Therefore atovaquone is the most appropriate option. The patient does not have an indication for Mycobacterium avium complex or Toxoplasma primary prophylaxis with the CD4 count at the current level.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q38

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman attended care to discuss immunizations. She had recently been diagnosed with HIV and had started ART 2 weeks previously. She denied a history of chickenpox or measles as a child. She reported 10 lifetime sexual partners. Investigations: CD4 count 115 cells/mm3 HIV-1 RNA viral load 145,000 copies/mL Hepatitis B surface Ag negative Hepatitis B surface Ab negative Hepatitis B core Ab positive Hepatitis B DNA <20 IU/mL VZV IgG negative Measles IgG negative
questions.lead_in: In addition to seasonal influenza vaccination, what immunizations should be offered?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus vaccine The patient has isolated hepatitis B virus (HBV) core antibody positivity but no evidence of chronic HBV or immunity to HBV based on negative HBV DNA and HBV surface antibody. Therefore HBV vaccination is indicated at this time even though the response rate may be lower given the low CD4 count. The patient’s CD4 count <200 cells/mm3 is a contraindication to live attenuated vaccines including herpes zoster (shingles), varicella (chickenpox), and measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccines. HPV vaccine is indicated for women through the age of 26 based on the licensing studies and since sexually active patients above this age are more likely to already have acquired HPV infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q37

parts.text: When should antiretroviral therapy be started, and why?
Give six screening tests indicated as part of her initial HIV assessment.

parts_raw.text: When to start ARVs? And why?
Give 6 screening tests indicated as part of her initial HIV assessment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Start ART within the first 2 weeks of beginning PCP treatment. Longer delay is associated with additional opportunistic infections and decreased survival; the exact day within that window depends on severity, ability to absorb oral drugs, and drug interactions. (PCP is not one of the exceptions - cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis is deferred 2-10 weeks; cryptosporidiosis and JC virus encephalitis are started as soon as feasible.) Caution: ART may worsen pulmonary function through IRIS as the recovering inflammatory response meets residual Pneumocystis antigen.
b) (1) Screening test for latent tuberculosis (TST or IGRA). (2) Toxoplasma gondii IgG serology (determines need for toxoplasmosis prophylaxis at CD4 <100). (3) Hepatitis B serology - anti-HBs/anti-HBc to define immunity and vaccination need (already immune here). (4) Hepatitis A serology to identify HAV-susceptible patients needing vaccination. (5) Coccidioides IgM/IgG serology if she lives in an endemic area (prophylaxis if positive and CD4 <250). (6) VZV serology/history of varicella or zoster to determine vaccine or post-exposure candidacy. Also: syphilis serology, and CD4 count/viral load monitoring to guide starting and stopping prophylaxis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Serum cryptococcal antigen screening at CD4 <100 and G6PD testing before dapsone are standard DHHS/IDSA OI-guideline additions not specified in this chapter text.

cohort_answer.text:
When to start ARVs: ASAP, within 2 weeks of dx of PCP – associated with lower death. In an RCT of 282 patients with OIs other than TB, 63% of whom had definite or presumptive PCP, a significantly lower incidence of AIDS progression or death (a secondary study endpoint) was seen in subjects randomized to early (median 12 days after initiation of therapy for OI) versus deferred initiation of ART (median 45 days). Of note, no patients with PCP and respiratory failure requiring intubation were enrolled in the study, and initiating ART in such patients is problematic due to the lack of parenteral preparations and unpredictble absorption of oral medications, as well as potential drug interactions with agents commonly used in the ICU
Six screening tests: Hep C serology; Baseline labs: CBC, LFTs, renal function; Cryptococcal antigen serum; TST / IGRA; Syphilis Screening; Gonorrhea and Chlamydia screen; HPV; VZV if no clear history of chicken pox +/- immunization; Toxo; G6PD screen (in case can't use TMP-SMX); Hep A (more in MSM)

questions.model_answer:
a) Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). ART-induced restoration of immune function produces an enhanced inflammatory response to residual organisms or antigen of an opportunistic pathogen, either paradoxically worsening a known infection or unmasking a subclinical one (e.g., MAC lymphadenitis, CMV retinitis) at sites not previously apparent.
b) (1) Severe immunosuppression at ART initiation (very low CD4 count with a high burden of untreated/subclinical opportunistic infection, e.g., mycobacterial or cryptococcal disease). (2) Rapid immunologic and virologic response after starting ART - starting ART early relative to opportunistic infection therapy, with a steep rise in CD4 count and fall in viral load.

cohort_answer.text:
Clinical syndrome: Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS). Increases in T lymphocytes after initiation of ART are also accompanied by increased in vitro lymphocyte proliferation responses, increased markers of immune activation, results in paradoxical worsening of infections or unmasking of infections secondary to host's regained capacity to mount an inflammatory response.
Two risk factors: extent of CD4+ T cell immune suppression prior to the initiation of ART; degree of viral suppression and immune recovery following the initiation of ART

questions.question: A patient is started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
questions.question_raw: A patient is started on HAART.

parts.text: Explain the pathogenesis of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
Name two risk factors.

parts_raw.text: Explain the pathogenesis of IRIS.
Name 2 risk factors.

questions.model_answer:
a) Potent ART rapidly suppresses HIV-1 RNA and raises CD4+ counts, producing at least partial immune reconstitution with return of pathogen-specific T-cell responses. Because recovery of antigen-specific immunity lags behind the CD4 rise and is dysregulated, the restored inflammatory response is directed against antigens of a persisting or recently treated pathogen (or its residual antigen), producing paradoxical clinical worsening of a previously silent, subclinical or adequately treated opportunistic infection (paradoxical IRIS) or unmasking of an undiagnosed one (unmasking IRIS). These reversal/unmasking reactions are analogous to reversal reactions in multibacillary leprosy: fever, focal lymphadenitis, worsening infiltrates or new inflammatory lesions typically 1 to 3 weeks (up to 1-2 months) after ART initiation. It is inflammation, not treatment failure; drug resistance, nonadherence, malabsorption, lymphoma and drug reaction must be excluded. Classically described with mycobacterial infection (tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium complex), and also with Cryptococcus neoformans, Pneumocystis jirovecii, PML, CMV (immune recovery uveitis/vitritis), Kaposi sarcoma and lymphoma; CNS IRIS carries the highest morbidity and mortality.
b) (1) Recent initiation of ART with a marked virologic/immunologic response (worsening typically within 2-3 weeks of starting therapy). (2) An underlying opportunistic infection with high antigen burden, particularly active or recently treated tuberculosis (incidence of tuberculosis IRIS 7%-43%), and, by extension, advanced immunosuppression with a low baseline CD4+ count.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell states IRIS risk factors are "not well understood"; low baseline CD4 count, high pre-ART viral load, high pathogen burden and short interval between OI treatment and ART start come from DHHS/IDSA opportunistic infection guidance.

What are potential treatments for IRIS

questions.model_answer:
a) IRIS is a clinically apparent, enhanced inflammatory response occurring after ART is started, as immune function is restored: it either paradoxically worsens a known opportunistic infection (e.g., raised ICP in cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis) or unmasks a subclinical infection with latent organisms or residual antigen (e.g., CMV retinitis, MAC lymphadenitis). It may be mild and self-limiting or life-threatening, and can be hard to distinguish from a new opportunistic infection or treatment failure.
b) (1) Profound pre-ART immunosuppression - very low CD4 count with a high burden of untreated opportunistic infection/antigen (as here, CD4 7). (2) High pre-ART viral load with a brisk virologic and immunologic response after ART - the rapid fall in viral load and rise in CD4 drives the inflammatory response; short interval from opportunistic-infection therapy to ART.
c) (1) Cryptococcus neoformans. (2) Toxoplasma gondii. (3) Mycobacterium tuberculosis. (4) JC virus (JC polyomavirus encephalitis/PML). Also consider cytomegalovirus.
d) Continue effective ART and specific antimicrobial therapy for the underlying pathogen. Mild/moderate paradoxical IRIS: NSAIDs without changing the OI or HIV regimen. Severe IRIS: systemic corticosteroids - e.g., for TB-IRIS prednisone 1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks then 0.75 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks (1.0 then 0.5 mg/kg/day if on rifabutin), tapered over 4 weeks or longer; for MAC-IRIS short-term (4-8 weeks) prednisone 20-40 mg equivalent. Corticosteroids may also be used for management of cryptococcal IRIS (though not for routine induction) and for presumed CMV IRIS. Manage raised ICP with repeated lumbar punctures or a CSF shunt - steroids and mannitol are ineffective for ICP. Severe refractory cases may warrant immunosuppressive biologic agents.

questions.model_answer:
a) An enhanced inflammatory response following ART-induced immune reconstitution, causing paradoxical worsening of a treated opportunistic infection or unmasking of a previously subclinical one; presentations range from mild and self-limiting to life-threatening.

cohort_answer.text: IRIS is a paradoxical worsening of an infectious syndrome, often after initiating treatment, as the immune system reconstitutes. Risk factors: Severe immunosuppression (low CD4); High viral load; Fungal infections (PJP).

questions.question: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in a patient with HIV infection.
questions.question_raw: 16. IRIS in an HIV patient

parts.text: What is the pathophysiology?
What are risk factors and how is it treated?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the pathophysiology?
b) What are risk factors and how is it treated?

questions.model_answer:
a) ART restores immune function, and the reconstituted immune and inflammatory response reacts against residual organisms or persisting antigen of an opportunistic pathogen. Two patterns: paradoxical IRIS - worsening of a recognized, already-treated infection (e.g., exacerbated pulmonary dysfunction when ART follows PCP therapy; raised ICP in cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis); and unmasking IRIS - clinical appearance of a subclinical infection not previously known (CMV retinitis, MAC lymphadenitis). IRIS may involve sites that appeared uninvolved at diagnosis (e.g., TB presenting as meningitis, pericarditis, or lymphadenitis).
b) Risk factors: profound immunosuppression with very low CD4 count and high viral load before ART; a high burden of untreated or subclinical opportunistic infection, especially mycobacterial and cryptococcal disease (about 30% of cryptococcal meningitis patients develop IRIS with ART) and CNS involvement; short interval between starting OI therapy and ART; rapid immunologic/virologic response to ART.
Treatment: continue ART and treat the underlying pathogen; NSAIDs for non-severe paradoxical IRIS; corticosteroids for severe disease (e.g., TB-IRIS prednisone 1.5 mg/kg/day x 2 weeks then 0.75 mg/kg/day x 2 weeks, tapered over at least 4 weeks; MAC-IRIS prednisone 20-40 mg for 4-8 weeks); repeated LPs or CSF shunting for raised ICP; immunosuppressive biologic agents in refractory cases. Prevention: defer ART 2-10 weeks in cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis, and 2-4 weeks in disseminated MAC.

cohort_answer.text:
Excessive immune reaction to a pre-existing infection, usually opportunistic, once immune system is reconstituted from AIDS. Paradoxical - symptoms worsen with immune reconstitution. Unmasking IRIS: appearance of new symptoms of an unrecognized preexisting pathogen upon immune reconstitution
Patient risk factors: Low CD4 T-cell count, high VL, CNS disease with TB/Crypto/other OI. Drug RFs: potency of ARV (integrase inhibitors > PI's > others). Infectious RFs: 29% Kaposi's sarcoma, 16% TB, 14% Crypto, 10% MAC, 4% Pneumocystis. Treatment: supportive - steroids or NSAIDs, continue ARV and treat underlying disease

questions.model_answer:
a) An exaggerated inflammatory response occurring after ART-induced immune reconstitution, directed at residual organisms or antigen of an opportunistic pathogen. Paradoxical IRIS worsens a recognized infection (e.g., raised ICP in cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis, worsening pulmonary function after PCP); unmasking IRIS reveals a subclinical infection such as CMV retinitis or MAC lymphadenitis. Ranges from mild and self-limiting to life-threatening and mimics both new opportunistic infection and treatment failure.
b) (1) Very low CD4 count with high viral load and a large untreated/subclinical opportunistic-infection burden, particularly CNS cryptococcal or tuberculous disease. (2) Early ART initiation relative to opportunistic-infection therapy, with rapid virologic suppression and CD4 recovery.
c) (1) Cryptococcus neoformans. (2) Toxoplasma gondii. (3) Mycobacterium tuberculosis. (4) JC virus (PML). Cytomegalovirus is an additional consideration.
d) Continue ART and pathogen-directed therapy. NSAIDs for non-severe IRIS. For severe or CNS IRIS, corticosteroids - e.g., prednisone 1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks then 0.75 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks with taper over at least 4 weeks (TB-IRIS regimen); corticosteroids are indicated in cryptococcal disease specifically for management of IRIS. Control raised ICP with repeated lumbar punctures or CSF shunting (corticosteroids and mannitol do not reduce ICP). Immunosuppressive biologic agents for refractory life-threatening IRIS.

cohort_answer.text: IRIS description: An exaggerated inflammatory reaction to a disease-causing organism that may occur during immune reconstitution (recovery) following initiation of ARVs. Two forms occur: 'unmasking' IRIS where new symptoms of an undiagnosed infection appear, and 'paradoxical' IRIS, where a previously treated infection worsens after ARV therapy is started (https://clinicalinfo.hiv.gov/en/glossary/immune-reconstitution-inflammatory-syndrome-iris). Risk factors: Low CD4 count (<100); High Viral Load (early initiation of ARV before treatment of infection). Pathogens: Cryptococcus neoformans; JCV (PML-IRIS); Mycobacterium Tuberculosis; Toxoplasma; MAC; CMV (immune recovery uveitis). Treatment: 0.5-1mg/kg/day Prednisone equivalent as Dexamethasone, tapered over 2-6 weeks depending on clinical improvement (IDSA Cryptococcus 2010)

parts_raw.text: 3 (or 4) infections for which primary prophylaxis is indicated, and CD4 cut-off. Medication and dose for each

questions.model_answer:
(1) Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia - CD4 <200 cells/mm3 (or CD4 <14%, or 200-250 if CD4 cannot be monitored q3 months) - TMP-SMZ 1 DS PO daily (or 1 SS PO daily). (2) Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis - Toxoplasma IgG-positive with CD4 <100 cells/mm3 - TMP-SMZ 1 DS PO daily (this also covers PCP). (3) Histoplasma capsulatum - CD4 <=150 cells/mm3 with occupational exposure or residence in a hyperendemic community (>10 cases/100 patient-years) - itraconazole 200 mg PO daily. (4) Coccidioidomycosis - new positive IgM or IgG serology in a patient living in an endemic area with CD4 <250 cells/mm3 - fluconazole 400 mg PO daily.
Note: MAC chemoprophylaxis at CD4 <50 (azithromycin) is no longer recommended, because all patients should start ART promptly and MAC has become rare. Latent TB treatment (INH 300 mg + pyridoxine daily x 9 months) is indicated at any CD4 count if the LTBI screen is positive or after close contact with infectious TB.

questions.question: Vaccines in HIV.
questions.question_raw: Vaccines in HIV

parts.text: List seven vaccinations in patients with HIV and CD4 count less than 100 cells/µL.

parts_raw.text: List 7 vaccinations in patients with HIV and CD4 <100

questions.model_answer: All must be non-live (live vaccines are contraindicated at CD4 <200). (1) Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23). (2) Hepatitis B vaccine — high/double-dose or adjuvanted schedule, with post-vaccination anti-HBs testing. (3) Hepatitis A vaccine. (4) Quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (Men-C-ACYW), 2-dose primary series with boosters, plus MenB vaccine. (5) Inactivated seasonal influenza vaccine, annually. (6) Tdap/Td (with subsequent Td boosters) and inactivated polio vaccine as needed for primary series completion. (7) HPV vaccine (9-valent, 3-dose schedule). Also indicated: recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix, non-live) and COVID-19 vaccine; Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine may be given if not previously immunized. Note that immunogenicity is poor at CD4 <100 — re-immunize or check serology after immune reconstitution on ART.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA/NIH OI guidelines and NACI Immunization of Immunocompromised Persons: live vaccines contraindicated at CD4 <200; recombinant zoster vaccine now replaces live zoster vaccine.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer lists "inactivated zoster vaccine (>50yo)" and Hib — the correct current product is recombinant adjuvanted zoster vaccine (Shingrix), recommended from age 18 in HIV, and Hib is no longer routinely recommended for adults with HIV alone.

cohort_answer.text: HIV related vaccines: Pneumococcal (Prevnar and pneumovax); Hepatitis B vaccine (double dose); Meningococcal conjugate vaccine; Haemophilus influenzae B vaccine; Hepatitis A vaccine. General population: Inactivated seasonal influenza; Diphtheria/tetanus; Pertussis; Inactivated polio; HPV vaccine; Inactivated zoster vaccine (>50yo). No live vaccines for CD4<200

questions.model_answer: IRIS is an enhanced inflammatory response after ART-induced immune reconstitution, directed at residual organisms or persisting antigen of an opportunistic pathogen. Two types: (1) Paradoxical IRIS - worsening of an already recognized and treated infection (e.g., worsening pulmonary dysfunction after PCP therapy, raised ICP in cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis), sometimes at sites that did not appear involved initially (TB meningitis, pericarditis, lymphadenitis). (2) Unmasking IRIS - clinical appearance of a previously subclinical or unrecognized infection (e.g., CMV retinitis, MAC lymphadenitis).

cohort_answer.text: IRIS describes a collection of inflammatory disorders associated with paradoxical worsening of preexisting infectious processes following initiation of ART. Paradoxical – worsening of recognized condition with lifting of immunosuppression; Unmasking – worsening of unrecognized condition that was pre-existing

parts.text: Describe the pathogenesis.

parts_raw.text: Describe the pathogenesis

questions.model_answer: a) Effective ART suppresses HIV replication and rapidly restores CD4+ T-cell number and pathogen-specific immune function (memory responses first, later naive-cell repopulation). The recovering immune system mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against residual viable organisms or persisting microbial antigen at sites of established or subclinical infection. The result is clinically apparent inflammation rather than uncontrolled infection: paradoxical worsening at a treated site (e.g., exacerbated pulmonary dysfunction with remaining Pneumocystis antigen; rising ICP with cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis), or unmasking of a previously subclinical focus (e.g., CMV retinitis, MAC lymphadenitis, TB meningitis/pericarditis/lymphadenitis in a patient treated for pulmonary TB). Manifestations range from mild and self-limited to life-threatening, are hard to distinguish from treatment failure or a new opportunistic infection, and may require corticosteroids or immunosuppressive biologics.

cohort_answer.text: Immune reconstitution of CD4 T-cells, initially memory but then also naïve, leads to rapid lymphocyte proliferation, increased markers of immune activation and pathogen-specific delayed hypersensitivity

questions.question: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in HIV infection.
questions.question_raw: IRIS

parts.text: List three risk factors.

parts_raw.text: 3 risk factors

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Advanced immunosuppression with a low CD4+ T-cell count at ART initiation (e.g., disseminated MAC or CMV disease occurring at CD4+ <50 cells/mm3). (2) A high baseline HIV viral load with rapid virologic suppression and steep immune recovery after starting ART. (3) The presence of an untreated or recently treated opportunistic infection with a high residual organism/antigen burden, particularly mycobacterial and fungal disease (tuberculosis, cryptococcal meningitis — about 30% develop IRIS — and MAC), especially when ART is begun early in its course.

cohort_answer.text: Low CD4 at start of tx; High VL; Rapid reduction in VL (e.g. with INSTI); Fungal OI

questions.question: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in HIV infection.
questions.question_raw: IRIS

parts.text: Name two clinical situations in which you might see IRIS.

parts_raw.text: What are 2 clinical situations where you might see IRIS?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Cryptococcal meningitis: ART started early after diagnosis provokes IRIS in about 30%, with headache, fever, photophobia, raised intracranial pressure, obtundation, herniation and death; hence ART is deferred to 2-10 weeks after starting antifungal therapy. (2) Tuberculosis: paradoxical worsening after ART, including new meningitis, pericarditis or lymphadenitis in a patient being treated for pulmonary TB, or unmasking of previously unrecognized TB. Other examples in the chapter: CMV retinitis/vitritis and MAC lymphadenitis appearing after ART initiation.

cohort_answer.text: HIV + cryptococcal meningitis; TB – esp CNS TB. Also described in HIV-uninfected patients following treatment for tuberculosis or lepromatous leprosy

questions.question: A patient with pulmonary tuberculosis starts treatment including rifampin. She has newly diagnosed HIV.
questions.question_raw: A patient with pulmonary TB starts on tx including rifampin. She has newly dx HIV.

parts.text: When should she start antiretroviral therapy if her CD4 count is 20 versus 85?

parts_raw.text: When should she start her ARV tx if her CD4 count is 20 vs 85?

questions.model_answer: a) Both should start early, since Mandell's general rule for an ART-naive patient with an acute opportunistic infection is to begin ART within the first 2 weeks of starting treatment for that infection, because longer delay is associated with additional opportunistic infections and decreased survival. With CD4 20 cells/mm3 (profound immunosuppression, highest risk of new opportunistic infection and death) start as soon as feasible, within 2 weeks of beginning anti-TB therapy. With CD4 85 cells/mm3 the same early-initiation principle applies but the urgency is lower, so ART can reasonably be started within about 8 weeks, allowing tolerance of TB therapy to be established and IRIS risk reduced. In either case the exception is tuberculous meningitis, where ART should be deferred (roughly 2-10 weeks), and rifampin-ART interactions must be managed (rifabutin substitution or dose adjustment, with therapeutic drug monitoring considered).
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS/IDSA OI guidelines supply the CD4 threshold used here: ART within 2 weeks if CD4 <50 cells/mm3 and within 8 weeks if CD4 >=50 (ACTG A5221 STRIDE, SAPiT, CAMELIA); Mandell states only the general 2-week rule.

cohort_answer.text: CD4=20 -> start ASAP within 2 weeks of anti-TB tx; CD4=85 -> start within 8 weeks of anti-TB tx. If CD4<50: start ART within 2 weeks; if CD4>50, start within 8 weeks; if CNS TB, delay ART for 8 weeks

questions.question: A woman with newly diagnosed HIV has a CD4 count of 65, a very high viral load and negative hepatitis B serology. She is HLA-B*5701 positive and her genotype shows a K103 mutation. She has been diagnosed with Pneumocystis pneumonia and is on treatment.
questions.question_raw: Woman with new dx of HIV, CD4 65, VL very high, HBV negative. HLAB5701 positive. Genotype shows K103 mutation. Dx with PCP pneumonia on treatment.

parts.text: When should she start antiretroviral therapy, and why?

parts_raw.text: When should she start ARVs and why?

questions.model_answer: a) Start ART early — within the first 2 weeks of beginning PCP treatment. Rationale: all patients with HIV should be treated expeditiously; deferring ART beyond this window in the setting of an acute opportunistic infection is associated with additional opportunistic infections and decreased survival, and immune augmentation aids recovery and prevents further HIV-related complications. PCP is not one of the exceptions (cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis, or clinically apparent pericardial disease) in which ART is delayed 2-10 weeks. She should be counselled that ART may worsen pulmonary function transiently through IRIS as recovering immunity reacts with residual Pneumocystis organisms/antigen, and the exact day within the window depends on severity, ability to absorb oral drugs and drug interactions. Regimen choice must avoid abacavir (HLA-B*5701 positive) and avoid NNRTIs given K103.
questions.beyond_mandell: The immediate-ART principle for all CD4 strata rests on START and TEMPRANO (2015); the ACTG A5164 trial supports early ART during acute PCP.

cohort_answer.text: Start immediately per START and TEMPRANO (2015) trials, especially in light of PCP pneumonia – will reduce morbidity and mortality

questions.question: A patient from Zimbabwe with tuberculosis was started on HRZE and then diagnosed with HIV (CD4 350). He presents with lung infiltrates and respiratory distress.
questions.question_raw: TB in Zimbabwe patient. Started on HRZE. Dx with HIV (CD4 350). Presents with lung infiltrates and resp distress.

parts.text: Give the likely reason.

parts_raw.text: Reason?

questions.model_answer: a) Most likely paradoxical TB-IRIS after ART initiation: restored pathogen-specific immunity mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response to residual mycobacterial antigen, producing worsening infiltrates and respiratory deterioration in a patient previously responding to TB therapy; IRIS may also involve sites not initially apparent (pleura, pericardium, nodes, CNS). Alternatives to exclude are progression or drug-resistant TB/treatment failure, a superimposed opportunistic infection such as Pneumocystis pneumonia or CMV pneumonitis, ordinary community-acquired pneumonia (HIV patients acquire non-opportunistic pathogens at least as often), and drug reaction.

cohort_answer.text: IRIS; paradoxical reaction of TB; PJP; CMV pneumonitis

questions.question: A patient from Zimbabwe with tuberculosis was started on HRZE and then diagnosed with HIV (CD4 350).
questions.question_raw: TB in Zimbabwe patient. Started on HRZE. Dx with HIV (CD4 350)

parts.text: Outline the management of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

parts_raw.text: Management of IRIS

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Confirm the diagnosis by excluding TB treatment failure/drug resistance, a new opportunistic infection and malignancy (biopsy or culture of an affected site when accessible). (2) Continue both anti-TB therapy and ART — IRIS is not a reason to stop either; interrupt ART only for compelling absorption or interaction problems. (3) For non-severe paradoxical IRIS, treat symptomatically with NSAIDs without changing TB or HIV therapy. (4) For severe IRIS, add prednisone with a taper over about 4 weeks — if on rifampin, 1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks then 0.75 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks (if on rifabutin, 1.0 then 0.5 mg/kg/day); a more gradual taper over months may be needed. (5) Provide site-specific supportive care (e.g., ICP management in CNS disease, drainage of pericardial or nodal collections) and consider immunosuppressive biologic agents for refractory life-threatening disease.

cohort_answer.text: Continue ARVs and anti-TB meds; Short course corticosteroids for severe symptoms

questions.question: A young woman from Zambia is found to have co-infection with HIV (CD4 350) and tuberculosis. What are three steps for immediate management?
questions.question_raw: Scenario involving young female from Zambia found to have co-infection with HIV (CD4 350) and TB

parts.text: What three steps for immediate management?

parts_raw.text: What 3 steps for immediate management?

questions.model_answer: (1) Start standard four-drug antituberculous therapy (RIPE) with pyridoxine, daily dosing, and send specimens for culture and drug-susceptibility testing (rule out CNS/disseminated TB). (2) Complete HIV staging — HIV viral load and resistance genotype — and plan a rifampin-compatible ART regimen; with CD4 350, start ART about 8 weeks after TB therapy (within 2 weeks if CD4 <50). (3) Screen for and manage co-morbidities/prophylaxis and monitor for IRIS and drug interactions/toxicity.

cohort_answer.text: Start RIPE; Get TB susceptibilities and rule out CNS TB; HIV viral load; HIV resistance genotype

questions.question: A young woman from Zambia is found to have co-infection with HIV (CD4 350) and tuberculosis.
questions.question_raw: Scenario involving young female from Zambia found to have co-infection with HIV (CD4 350) and TB

parts.text: What are the potential clinical problems if antiretroviral therapy is started 10 days after initiating tuberculosis medications?

parts_raw.text: What are potential clinical problems if starting ARVs 10 days after initiating TB medications?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) IRIS: rapid virologic suppression and immune restoration within the first weeks of ART provokes an exaggerated inflammatory response to residual mycobacterial antigen — paradoxical worsening in a patient who was improving (fever, worsening infiltrates, enlarging nodes) or unmasking of disease at sites not previously apparent (meningitis, pericarditis, lymphadenitis), which can be life threatening and is hard to distinguish from treatment failure or a new opportunistic infection. (2) Occult tuberculous meningitis or pericardial disease, in which early ART risks dangerously increased intracranial pressure; these are the explicit exceptions where ART is deferred until 2-10 weeks of anti-TB therapy have been given. (3) Overlapping drug toxicity and confusion of attribution — hepatitis, rash, cytopenias and gastrointestinal intolerance from concurrent TB drugs and ART, making it difficult to identify the offending agent and threatening adherence to both regimens. (4) Pharmacokinetic interactions: rifamycins substantially alter levels of protease inhibitors, NNRTIs and boosting agents, requiring rifabutin substitution or dose adjustment, with therapeutic drug monitoring considered.

cohort_answer.text: IRIS – rapid restoration of immune responses to opportunistic pathogens (mainly TB), usually within first 3 weeks of starting ART, causing clinical deterioration/inflammation. TB associated IRIS: Paradoxical IRIS (onset in patients already treated for TB, previously responding, develop new/worsening manifestations, usually advanced HIV + good immune response, can last ~2 months; 4 week course of Prednisone improves sx and decreases need for hospitalizations); Unmasking IRIS (onset in patients with previously unrecognized, untreated TB)

questions.question_raw: African woman with HIV CD4 350 with pulmonary TB.

parts_raw.text: 3 initial management steps

questions.model_answer: (1) Start standard RIPE antituberculous therapy with pyridoxine (daily dosing) and send cultures/drug-susceptibility testing; rule out CNS/disseminated TB. (2) HIV staging with viral load and resistance genotype, and plan rifampin-compatible ART — with CD4 350 initiate ART ~8 weeks after starting TB treatment. (3) Monitor for drug interactions, hepatotoxicity, and IRIS; provide appropriate co-infection prophylaxis.

questions.question: An African woman with HIV and a CD4 count of 350 has pulmonary tuberculosis.
questions.question_raw: African woman with HIV CD4 350 with pulmonary TB.

parts.text: What are two complications of starting HIV therapy at this point?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 complications of starting HIV therapy at this point?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) IRIS — an enhanced inflammatory response to residual mycobacterial antigen causing paradoxical clinical deterioration or unmasking of disease at previously unrecognized sites; occult tuberculous meningitis must be excluded first, because in that setting early ART can cause dangerously raised intracranial pressure and ART should be deferred until 2-10 weeks of TB therapy. (2) Drug-drug interactions and overlapping toxicity — rifampin induces hepatic cytochrome metabolism and markedly alters levels of protease inhibitors, NNRTIs and boosting agents (rifabutin substitution or dose adjustment and therapeutic drug monitoring are needed), while shared hepatotoxicity, rash and gastrointestinal intolerance across the two regimens complicate attribution and adherence.

cohort_answer.text: Need to rule out TB meningitis first – may trigger IRIS; Drug interactions with Rifampin

CD4 is 100.
questions.question_raw: Child from Zimbabwe, in Canada for one year. Fever and weight loss and FTT for 2 months, cough, CXR RLL infiltrate, sputum AFB + and Amplified Mycobacterium Tuberculosis Direct (AMTD) Test +. CD4 100.

parts_raw.text: A) 3 initial treatment considerations

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Assess for disseminated/CNS disease, which prolongs therapy (bone/joint 6-9 months, meningitis 9-12 months) and, for CNS/pericardial disease, warrants adjunctive corticosteroids. (2) Risk of drug resistance given a high-prevalence origin/index case - obtain susceptibility testing (and rifampin-resistance detection) and consider added agents pending results. (3) HIV co-management: choose a rifamycin-compatible regimen and anticipate drug-drug interactions and IRIS; also confirm ability to take/absorb oral medication.
b) Do not delay long - because CD4 is <50... in this child CD4 is 100, so start antiretrovirals within about 8 weeks of TB therapy (within 2 weeks if CD4 <50); persistent fever at 10 days is not itself an indication to start ART immediately, and TB therapy should be established first.
c) (1) Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS/paradoxical reaction). (2) Drug-drug interactions (rifampin with antiretrovirals) and overlapping toxicities/pill burden.
d) In this chapter XDR-TB is defined as resistance to INH, RIF, any fluoroquinolone, and at least one of three injectable second-line drugs (amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin).
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort gives the revised 2021 WHO XDR-TB definition (resistance to INH, RIF, any fluoroquinolone, plus a Group A drug such as bedaquiline or linezolid); the Mandell text uses the older definition (INH, RIF, a fluoroquinolone, plus an injectable second-line agent).

questions.model_answer: a) A lymphocytic-predominant CSF in an African patient with advanced HIV: (1) tuberculous meningitis; (2) CNS toxoplasmosis; (3) CNS lymphoma (other opportunistic CNS infection is also reasonable). b) (1) Relieve raised intracranial pressure with a therapeutic/large-volume lumbar puncture (CSF drainage or shunt if refractory); (2) protect the airway and begin induction antifungal therapy (amphotericin B plus flucytosine) urgently. c) Induction: amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks; consolidation: fluconazole 400-800 mg/day for 8-10 weeks; suppression/maintenance: fluconazole 200 mg once daily. d) Delay ART rather than starting it at diagnosis: begin roughly 4-6 weeks (about 5 weeks) after antifungal therapy is started, because early ART increases cryptococcal IRIS and mortality; the improving immune response mobilizes inflammation against residual yeast/antigen. e) (1) India ink stain; (2) cryptococcal antigen (CrAg); (3) fungal culture (plus opening pressure and cell count/glucose/protein).
questions.beyond_mandell: ART timing (delay ~4-6 weeks; COAT trial and WHO/IDSA guidance) is not in the chapter text, which describes cryptococcal IRIS but not the optimal delay.

Syphilis, toxo, TB
Decrease intracranial pressure with LP/shunt; Manage/protect airway – intubate; Urgent CT to look for herniation
Amphotericin B + flucytosine x 2 weeks then fluconazole 400mg x 8 weeks; Fluconazole 200mg daily until CD4 >100, VL undetectable for >=3mos, at least 12 mos of tx
2-10 weeks after starting treatment to prevent IRIS
Cryptococcal antigen, fungal culture; Opening pressures (if high, do daily LPs do relieve or if requires VPS/EVD)

questions.model_answer: a) Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO loading dose, then 50 mg/day (<60 kg) to 75 mg/day (>=60 kg), PLUS sulfadiazine 1000 mg (<60 kg) to 1500 mg (>=60 kg) q6h, PLUS folinic acid (leucovorin) 10-20 mg/day (up to 50 mg/day); acute therapy for at least 3-6 weeks, followed by maintenance (secondary prophylaxis). b) At 16 weeks (>=14 weeks) pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid is acceptable, so the same regimen can be used (pyrimethamine is avoided only in the first trimester); pyrimethamine-clindamycin-folinic acid is an alternative. c) Primary CNS lymphoma.

cohort_answer.text: First line therapy: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin for 6 weeks, followed by TMP/SMX 1 DS BID until VL suppressed and CD4 >200 for 3 months (if unable to use sulfadiazine need alternative PJP proph agent). If pregnant: HIV+ with brain lesions + pregnant = wait until 2nd trimester to use pyrimethamine, otherwise treat as per adult; discuss risks/benefits of secondary prophylaxis with TMPSMX during pregnancy; spiramycin recommended to prevent congenital transmission during primary infection in pregnancy but does not treat fetal infection; pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin recommended for pregnant women with strong suspicion of fetal infection, pyrimethamine avoided in first trimester due to teratogenicity. Top differential: Primary CNS lymphoma (median age 35 in HIV, often multiple lesions); other ddx: TB, PML (white matter lesions), Cryptococcal meningitis (not typical imaging), Neurocysticercosis (no travel), Bartonellosis (no exposures)

questions.question: A very sick patient with HIV and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CD4 60, viral load >180,000, HLA-B*5701 positive, K103N mutation present.
questions.question_raw: PM Q10. Very sick patient, HIV (+), PJP, CD4 60, VL >180K, HLA B5701(+), K103N mutation (+)

parts.text: Give 3 first line regimens that could be used
When should you look to start ART considering the PJP pneumonia?

parts_raw.text: a) Give 3 first line regimens that could be used
b) When should you look to start ART considering the PJP pneumonia?

questions.model_answer:
a) HLA-B*5701 positive excludes abacavir, and K103N abolishes efavirenz and nevirapine activity (rilpivirine is also excluded by the viral load >100,000 and CD4 <200), so use an INSTI plus a tenofovir prodrug-emtricitabine backbone: (1) dolutegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)-emtricitabine; (2) coformulated bictegravir-TAF-emtricitabine; (3) raltegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)-emtricitabine.
b) Start early rather than deferring. Acute opportunistic infection and a CD4 <200 cells/mm3 are conditions favoring early initiation, ART is recommended for all regardless of CD4, and rapid (including same-day) initiation shortens time to virologic suppression and improves retention in care. Begin once the patient is stable on anti-Pneumocystis therapy and able to take oral medication, alongside corticosteroids for severe PJP.
questions.beyond_mandell: ACTG A5164: starting ART within ~2 weeks of an acute OI such as PJP reduced AIDS progression/death; cryptococcal and TB meningitis are the recognized exceptions where ART is delayed.

cohort_answer.text:
K103N reduces NNRTI efficacy (efavirenz, nevirapine) by 20-50x, no effect on rilpivirine (but VL too high) or doravirine. DTG + (TDF or TAF) + FTC; BIC + TAF + FTC; RAL + TAF or TDF + FTC; DOR + TAF or TDF + FTC
No need to delay; in fact, increased mortality with delay. ONLY reasons to delay are crypto meningitis and TB meningitis

questions.question: A man with HIV and CD4 <50 had stopped co-trimoxazole (septra) because of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. He presents with 2 weeks of fever and neurologic symptoms. CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions without mass effect.
questions.question_raw: HIV man with CD4 <50. Had stopped Septra because of SJS. 2 weeks of fever and neurologic symptoms. CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What would you treat with and for how long? What secondary prophylaxis? When do you stop?

parts_raw.text: What to treat with and for how long? What secondary ppx? When do you stop?

questions.model_answer: Because of the sulfa allergy (SJS), avoid sulfadiazine and TMP-SMX. Treat with pyrimethamine (200 mg load, then 50-75 mg/day) PLUS clindamycin (600 mg q6h, up to 1200 mg q6h) PLUS folinic acid 10-20 mg/day. Acute therapy for at least 3 weeks and usually 6 weeks (longer if incomplete response). Follow with secondary prophylaxis (maintenance) using the same agents at reduced dose (pyrimethamine 25-50 mg/day plus clindamycin 600 mg q8h plus folinic acid). Because clindamycin-pyrimethamine has no anti-Pneumocystis activity, add PCP prophylaxis (e.g., atovaquone or aerosolized pentamidine). Stop maintenance therapy when CD4 rises above 200 cells/mm3 and is sustained for at least 6 months on ART with resolution of disease.

cohort_answer.text: Toxoplasmosis gondii. HIV+ CD4<100 with space-occupying lesion involving gray matter: ddx is either toxo or lymphoma. If in endemic area: fungal, mycobacterial and parasitic also possible

questions.question: A patient with newly diagnosed HIV, recently arrived from Africa, has cryptococcal meningitis. When should antiretroviral therapy be started? Explain your answer.
questions.question_raw: Cryptococcal meningitis in newly diagnosed HIV from Africa.

parts.text: When should antiretroviral therapy be started? Explain your answer.

parts_raw.text: When should ART be started? Explain your answer

questions.model_answer: a) Do not start ART at diagnosis - delay it roughly 4-6 weeks (about 5 weeks) after antifungal therapy is begun. Early ART worsens outcomes by precipitating cryptococcal IRIS (the COAT trial showed higher mortality with early ART); a low baseline CSF WBC marks the highest IRIS risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: ART-timing evidence (COAT trial; WHO/IDSA delay of ~4-6 weeks) is not in the chapter text, which describes IRIS but not the optimal ART delay.

cohort_answer.text: Earlier ART can be detrimental in CNS infections. Delay ARV by at least 5 weeks per COAT trial to reduce risk of cryptococcal IRIS. Low CSF WBC count at diagnosis associated with greatest risk of IRIS with ART initiation
